l: Pelias, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Pelias was exposed with his twin brother Neleus and was rescued and raised by a horse-keeper after a mare left a livid mark on his face. He and Neleus later recognized Tyro and killed their stepmother Sidero, with Pelias cutting her down at Hera’s altars. Pelias dwelt in Thessaly and had a son, Acastus, and daughters including Alcestis.

l: Neleus, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Neleus was exposed with Pelias, rescued by a horse-keeper, and raised with him. After recognizing Tyro, he helped kill their stepmother Sidero, but later quarreled with Pelias and was banished. He went to Messene, founded Pylus, married Chloris, and fathered Pero, Nestor, and other children.

l: Pylus, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Pylus was founded by Neleus in Messene. Heracles later ravaged Pylus, killing Neleus’s sons except Nestor.

l: Nestor, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Nestor was the only one of Neleus’s sons to survive Heracles’s attack on Pylus because he had been brought up among the Gerenians. He married Anaxibia and fathered several daughters and sons.

l: Hercules, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Heracles ravaged Pylus and killed Neleus’s sons, including Periclymenus, while Nestor alone was saved.

l: Bias, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Bias, son of Amythaon, wooed Pero, daughter of Neleus. Because Neleus required a suitor to bring him the kine of Phylacus, Bias asked his brother Melampus for help. After Melampus obtained the kine, Bias received Pero and later had a son, Talaus, with her.

l: Amythaon, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Amythaon was a son of Cretheus and Tyro. He dwelt in Pylus and married Idomene, daughter of Pheres; their sons were Bias and Melampus.

l: Melampus, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Melampus learned to understand the voices of birds after raising young snakes whose tongues purged his ears while he slept, and he became an excellent soothsayer. He obtained the kine of Phylacus for his brother Bias after being detected stealing them and kept in bondage for a year. He later healed the women of Argos whom Dionysus had driven mad and settled there with Bias.

l: kine of Phylacus, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: The kine of Phylacus were guarded by a dog that no person or beast could approach. Melampus stole them for Bias, was detected and imprisoned for a year, and then drove the kine to Pylus so that Bias could receive Pero.

l: Adrastus, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Adrastus was a son of Talaus and Lysimache, and therefore a descendant of Bias and Pero. With Amphithea, daughter of Pronax, he fathered Argia, Deipyle, Aegialia, Aegialeus, and Cyanippus.

l: Admetus, The Library, Now Tyro, daughter of Salmoneus and Alcidice,
s: Admetus was a son of Pheres, son of Cretheus. He reigned over Pherae, and Apollo served him as a thrall.

l: The Library, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Pelias promised Alcestis to the man who could yoke a lion and a boar, and Apollo enabled Admetus to win her. After Admetus forgot Artemis at his marriage sacrifice, he was granted release from death if someone voluntarily died for him, and Alcestis did so; she was later restored according to one account by the Maiden and according to another by Hercules. Pelias later learned from an oracle to beware the one-sandaled man, and Jason became that man while crossing the Anaurus; Pelias therefore sent him to fetch the Golden Fleece from Colchis. Jason gathered the Argonauts aboard the Argo, whose voyage included Lemnos and Mysia, where Hercules and Polyphemus were left behind after Hylas disappeared.

l: Alcestis, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Alcestis, daughter of Pelias, was obtained by Admetus after he yoked a lion and a boar to a car. When Admetus was destined to die, neither his father nor his mother would die for him, but Alcestis voluntarily died in his stead. She was later sent back according to one account, while another says that Hercules brought her back after fighting Hades.

l: Pelias, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Pelias promised Alcestis to the man who could yoke a lion and a boar to a car, and Admetus fulfilled the condition. He was warned by an oracle to beware of the one-sandaled man and later recognized Jason as that man. After Jason proposed sending someone for the Golden Fleece, Pelias ordered Jason to fetch it from Colchis.

l: Admetus, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Admetus yoked a lion and a boar with Apollo's help, brought them to Pelias, and obtained Alcestis. After forgetting to sacrifice to Artemis at his marriage, he found his marriage chamber filled with coiled snakes. He was granted release from death if someone voluntarily died for him, and Alcestis died in his place.

l: Hercules, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Hercules is said to have fought Hades and brought Alcestis back to Admetus. During the voyage of the Argo, he was left behind in Mysia while searching for Hylas; one account instead says he did not sail then, another that he was left at Aphetae, and another that he reached Colchis and became a leader of the Argonauts.

l: Jason, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Jason lived in Iolcus and lost one sandal while crossing the Anaurus, thereby becoming the man of Pelias's oracle. When asked what he would do if a citizen were destined to kill a king, he answered that he would send the man to fetch the Golden Fleece, and Pelias immediately sent Jason on that quest. Jason summoned Argus to build the Argo and led the assembled Argonauts on their voyage; he also slept with Hypsipyle and fathered Euneus and Nebrophonus.

l: Colchis, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Colchis was the place where the Golden Fleece hung from an oak in a grove of Ares. The fleece was guarded by a sleepless dragon, and Jason was sent there to obtain it.

l: Golden Fleece, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: The Golden Fleece was located in Colchis, hanging from an oak in a grove of Ares and guarded by a sleepless dragon. Pelias ordered Jason to bring it back.

l: Argonauts, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: The Argonauts were the nobles and heroes of Greece assembled for Jason's expedition to the Golden Fleece. They sailed in the Argo, stopped at Lemnos, fought the Doliones by mistake, and later reached Mysia, where Hercules and Polyphemus were left behind.

l: Argo, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Argus built the Argo as a ship with fifty oars, naming it after its builder. Athena fitted a speaking timber from the oak of Dodona into its prow. The Argo carried Jason and the Argonauts on their voyage toward Colchis and later departed while Hercules and Polyphemus were searching for Hylas.

l: Polyphemus, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Polyphemus heard Hylas cry out in Mysia and pursued him with a drawn sword, thinking robbers were carrying him away. He encountered Hercules and informed him of what had happened, but the Argo departed while they searched for Hylas. Polyphemus remained in Mysia, founded the city of Cius, and became its king.

l: Lemnos, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Lemnos was temporarily without men and was ruled by Hypsipyle. The Argonauts stopped there, had intercourse with the women, and then sailed onward.

l: Hypsipyle, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Hypsipyle, daughter of Thoas, ruled Lemnos when it was without men. She alone saved her father during the killing of the fathers and husbands by hiding him. She slept with Jason and bore Euneus and Nebrophonus.

l: Lemnian women, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: The Lemnian women were afflicted by a noisome smell after failing to honor Aphrodite, and their husbands slept with captive women from Thrace. In response, they killed their fathers and husbands, except that Hypsipyle saved her own father. They later received the Argonauts and had intercourse with them.

l: Mysia, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Mysia was a place where the Argonauts stopped after burying Cyzicus. Hercules and Polyphemus were left there while searching for Hylas; Polyphemus founded Cius in Mysia and ruled it.

l: Hylas, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Hylas, son of Thiodamas and beloved by Hercules, was sent to draw water in Mysia. Nymphs carried him away because of his beauty after he cried out, and Hercules and Polyphemus searched for him.

l: marriage of Admetus and Alcestis, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: At the marriage of Admetus and Alcestis, Admetus forgot to sacrifice to Artemis. When he opened the marriage chamber, he found it filled with coils of snakes, and Apollo told him to appease the goddess.

l: oracle of the one-sandaled man, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: The oracle warned Pelias to beware of the man with a single sandal. Pelias initially failed to understand it but later recognized its meaning when Jason arrived wearing only one sandal.

l: single sandal, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Jason lost one sandal while crossing the Anaurus and emerged from the river wearing only one. This fulfilled the sign in the oracle that Pelias should beware of the one-sandaled man.

l: death-substitution for Admetus, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: Apollo obtained from the Fates the condition that Admetus could escape death if someone voluntarily died for him. When the appointed day came, neither Admetus's father nor his mother agreed to die, but Alcestis did so.

l: voyage to Colchis, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: The voyage of the Argo began after Jason assembled the Argonauts to seek the Golden Fleece in Colchis. The ship stopped at Lemnos, where Jason slept with Hypsipyle, then reached the land of the Doliones and Mysia. In Mysia, Hercules and Polyphemus were left behind while searching for Hylas.

l: massacre of the Lemnian men, The Library, Πελίον θυγατέρα Αλκηστιν. ἐκείνου 1 δὲ δώσειν
s: The Lemnian women killed their fathers and husbands after being dishonored by their husbands' intercourse with captive women from Thrace. Hypsipyle alone saved her own father, Thoas, by hiding him.

l: The Library, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: The Argonauts reach Salmydessus, where Phineus tells them how to escape the Harpies and pass the Clashing Rocks. They pass the rocks with the help of a dove and Hera, then travel to Colchis and ask Aeetes for the Golden Fleece. Medea promises Jason assistance after he swears to take her as his wife to Greece, and Jason uses her drug to yoke the brazen-footed bulls and defeat the armed men who rise from the dragon’s teeth.

l: Argo, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: The Argo carries the Argonauts to Salmydessus, through the Clashing Rocks, and onward to Colchis. Its prow is used to release a dove, and the tips of its ornamental fittings are cut off while it passes between the rocks.

l: Argonauts, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: The Argonauts arrive at Salmydessus and seek Phineus’s advice about their voyage. After helping free Phineus from the Harpies, they follow his instructions through the Clashing Rocks, reach Colchis, and accompany Jason during his tasks for Aeetes.

l: Phineus, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: Phineus is a seer living at Salmydessus who has lost the sight of both eyes. After the Argonauts free him from the Harpies, he tells them the route of their voyage and advises them how to pass the Clashing Rocks.

l: Colchis, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: Colchis is the land where the river Phasis is located and where the Argonauts arrive. Jason goes there to ask Aeetes for the Golden Fleece.

l: Harpies, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: The Harpies are winged creatures sent to Phineus by the gods. They repeatedly snatch most of the food placed before him and leave behind a stench-filled remainder, but Zetes and Calais pursue them through the air; one falls into the river Tigres, while the other reaches the Echinadian Islands.

l: the Wandering Rocks, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: The Clashing Rocks are enormous rocks that collide under the force of the winds and block the sea passage. Following Phineus’s advice, the Argonauts send a dove through them; after its tail is clipped, they pass through with hard rowing and Hera’s help, and the rocks thereafter stand still.

l: Jason, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: Jason asks Aeetes for the Golden Fleece and agrees to perform the required tasks. With Medea’s drug protecting him, he yokes the brazen-footed bulls and causes the armed men sprung from the dragon’s teeth to fight one another before killing them.

l: Aeetes, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: Aeetes is approached by Jason in Colchis concerning the Golden Fleece. He promises to give it to Jason if Jason alone yokes the brazen-footed bulls and sows the dragon’s teeth.

l: Golden Fleece, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: The Golden Fleece is sought by Jason in Colchis. Aeetes agrees to give it to Jason if he completes the tasks involving the brazen-footed bulls and the dragon’s teeth.

l: brazen-footed bulls, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: The brazen-footed bulls are two enormous, wild bulls gifted to Aeetes by Hephaestus. Their feet are made of bronze and they breathe fire from their mouths, but Jason protects himself with Medea’s drug and yokes them.

l: Medea, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: Medea, the daughter of Aeetes and Idyia, is skilled in magic and falls in love with Jason. Fearing that the bulls will destroy him, she secretly promises to help him yoke them and obtain the fleece.

l: drug, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: Medea gives Jason a drug and tells him to anoint his shield, spear, and body with it. The drug protects him for one day from harm by fire and iron.

l: Jason and Medea’s marriage pact, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: Medea promises to help Jason and give him the Golden Fleece if he swears to take her as his wife and bring her with him to Greece. Jason swears to fulfill this agreement.

l: yoking the bulls and sowing the dragon’s teeth, The Library, «ἐνύμρης;»} Βιθυνίδος. γενναῖος δὲ ὧν οὗτος τοὺς
s: Aeetes requires Jason to yoke the brazen-footed bulls and sow the dragon’s teeth. After Jason sows the teeth, armed men rise from the ground; he throws stones among them so that they fight one another, then approaches and kills them.

l: The Library, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Medea helps Jason obtain the fleece, escapes with him and Apsyrtus, and kills Apsyrtus when Aeetes pursues them. Zeus sends a storm because of Apsyrtus’s murder, and the Argonauts are purified by Circe before continuing their voyage through various dangers to Iolcus. Medea helps Jason bring about Pelias’s death, after which Jason and Medea are expelled from Iolcus and settle in Corinth. There, Jason marries Glauce, and Medea kills Glauce and her own children Mermerus and Pheres before fleeing to Athens.

l: Aeetes, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Aeetes refuses to give Jason the fleece because he wants to burn the Argo and kill its crew. After Medea and Jason escape, he pursues them, but Medea kills Apsyrtus and throws his dismembered limbs into the sea; while gathering them, Aeetes falls behind. He buries the recovered limbs, names the place Tomi, and sends Colchians to search for the Argo and Medea.

l: Medea, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Medea brings Jason to the fleece at night, puts its guarding dragon to sleep with drugs, and escapes with Jason and Apsyrtus. She kills and dismembers Apsyrtus when Aeetes approaches, and later helps Jason obtain revenge on Pelias by persuading Pelias’s daughters to cut up and boil their father. In Corinth she is divorced by Jason, sends Glauce a poisoned robe that kills Glauce and Creon, kills Mermerus and Pheres, and flees to Athens in a chariot from the Sun drawn by winged dragons.

l: Jason, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Jason obtains the fleece with Medea’s help and escapes from Colchis with her and Apsyrtus. He travels with the Argonauts, is purified by Circe for the murder of Apsyrtus, and returns to Iolcus. He gives the fleece to Pelias, later asks Medea to devise revenge against him, and eventually marries Glauce in Corinth after divorcing Medea.

l: Apsyrtus, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Apsyrtus accompanies Medea and Jason aboard the Argo when they flee by night. Medea kills him, cuts him into pieces, and throws them into the sea. His murder causes Zeus to send a storm and requires the Argonauts to be purified by Circe.

l: Argonauts, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: The Argonauts put to sea by night with Jason, Medea, and Apsyrtus after the fleece is taken. They are driven off course by a storm sent because of Apsyrtus’s murder and are purified by Circe. They pass the Ligurians, Celts, Sirens, Charybdis, Scylla, the Wandering Rocks, Thrinacia, and Crete before reaching Iolcus after a four-month voyage.

l: Argo, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: The Argo is the ship on which Jason, Medea, Apsyrtus, and the Argonauts escape from Colchis. It is pursued by Aeetes, later speaks near the Apsyrtides Islands about the need for purification, and is guided through dangerous waters by Thetis and the Nereids. Jason eventually dedicates it to Poseidon at the Isthmus.

l: Golden Fleece, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Aeetes refuses to give the fleece to Jason. Medea leads Jason to it at night, helps him overcome its guarding dragon, and escapes with it to the Argo. Jason later gives the fleece to Pelias after returning to Iolcus.

l: the Colchians, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Aeetes sends many Colchians to search for the Argo and Medea, threatening them with Medea’s punishment if they fail to bring her back. They separate and search in different places; some settle near the Ceraunian mountains, some colonize the Apsyrtides Islands in Illyria, and others reach the Phaeacians. Those who find the Argo at the Phaeacians demand Medea from Alcinous, but afterward the Colchians settle among the Phaeacians.

l: Zeus, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Zeus sends a violent storm against the Argonauts because he is angry over the murder of Apsyrtus. The Argo declares that his anger will not cease until the Argonauts are purified by Circe.

l: the murder of Apsyrtus, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: The murder of Apsyrtus is committed by Medea while Aeetes pursues the fleeing Argo. Zeus responds with anger and a storm, and the Argonauts must travel to Ausonia to be purified by Circe for the deed.

l: Talos, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Talos prevents the Argonauts from landing in Crete and throws stones at the approaching Argo. He is described as a brazen man or bull with one vein running from his neck to his ankles and a bronze nail at its end. Medea causes his death, according to differing accounts, by drugs, by removing the nail after promising immortality, or by inducing him to be shot in the ankle by Poeas.

l: Iolcus, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: The Argonauts return to Iolcus after completing their voyage in four months. Jason gives the fleece to Pelias there, and later Pelias’s death leads Acastus to expel Jason and Medea from Iolcus.

l: Pelias, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Pelias despairs of the Argonauts’ return and wants to kill Aeson. He dies after drinking bull’s blood while offering a sacrifice, though another account in the narrative concerns his later death at the hands of his daughters, whom Medea deceives into cutting him up and boiling him. His son Acastus buries him and expels Jason and Medea from Iolcus.

l: Aeson, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Aeson is threatened with death by Pelias when Pelias believes the Argonauts will not return. He asks to take his own life and dies while offering a sacrifice and drinking bull’s blood.

l: Corinth, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Jason and Medea settle in Corinth and live happily there for ten years. Their relationship ends when Jason marries Glauce, and Corinth becomes the scene of Medea’s revenge against Glauce, Creon, Mermerus, and Pheres.

l: Creon, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Creon is the king of Corinth and betroths his daughter Glauce to Jason. He dies in the fierce fire caused by Glauce’s poisoned robe when he goes to help her.

l: Glauce, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Glauce is the daughter of Creon and becomes Jason’s wife after he divorces Medea. Medea sends her a robe steeped in poison, and Glauce is consumed by fierce fire when she puts it on.

l: Mermerus, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Mermerus is one of the children Medea has with Jason. Medea kills him before fleeing Corinth.

l: Pheres, The Library, τῶν ταύρων οὐκ ἐδίδου τὸ δέρας Αἰήτης, ἐβούλετο
s: Pheres is one of the children Medea has with Jason. Medea kills him before fleeing Corinth.

l: The Library, The Library, τῆς “Hpas τῆς ἀκραίας" ἹΚορίνθιοι δὲ αὐτοὺς ava-
s: Medea came to Athens, married Aegeus, and bore a son named Medus. She later plotted against Theseus and was driven from Athens with Medus. Medus conquered many barbarians, named the territory under him Media, and died while campaigning against the Indians. Medea returned to Colchis, killed Perses after finding that he had deposed Aeetes, and restored the kingdom to Aeetes.

l: Medea, The Library, τῆς “Hpas τῆς ἀκραίας" ἹΚορίνθιοι δὲ αὐτοὺς ava-
s: Medea came to Athens and married Aegeus, with whom she had a son named Medus. She later plotted against Theseus and was driven from Athens with Medus. Medea returned unknown to Colchis, killed Perses, and restored the kingdom to Aeetes.

l: Athens, The Library, τῆς “Hpas τῆς ἀκραίας" ἹΚορίνθιοι δὲ αὐτοὺς ava-
s: Athens was where Medea came, married Aegeus, and bore Medus. Medea was later driven from Athens with her son.

l: Aegeus, The Library, τῆς “Hpas τῆς ἀκραίας" ἹΚορίνθιοι δὲ αὐτοὺς ava-
s: Aegeus married Medea in Athens, and Medea bore him a son named Medus.

l: Medus, The Library, τῆς “Hpas τῆς ἀκραίας" ἹΚορίνθιοι δὲ αὐτοὺς ava-
s: Medus was the son of Medea and Aegeus. He conquered many barbarians, called the country under him Media, and died while campaigning against the Indians.

l: Theseus, The Library, τῆς “Hpas τῆς ἀκραίας" ἹΚορίνθιοι δὲ αὐτοὺς ava-
s: Medea plotted against Theseus. She was subsequently driven from Athens with her son.

l: Media, The Library, τῆς “Hpas τῆς ἀκραίας" ἹΚορίνθιοι δὲ αὐτοὺς ava-
s: Media was the name Medus gave to the whole country under his control after he conquered many barbarians.

l: Colchis, The Library, τῆς “Hpas τῆς ἀκραίας" ἹΚορίνθιοι δὲ αὐτοὺς ava-
s: Medea came to Colchis unknown after leaving Athens.

l: Aeetes, The Library, τῆς “Hpas τῆς ἀκραίας" ἹΚορίνθιοι δὲ αὐτοὺς ava-
s: Aeetes had been deprived of his kingdom by his brother Perses. Medea killed Perses and restored the kingdom to Aeetes.

l: Perses, The Library, τῆς “Hpas τῆς ἀκραίας" ἹΚορίνθιοι δὲ αὐτοὺς ava-
s: Perses had deposed his brother Aeetes and taken his kingdom. Medea killed Perses and restored the kingdom to Aeetes.

l: The Library, The Library, BOOK ITI
s: The unit traces the Inachean family from Inachus, son of Ocean and Tethys, through Phoroneus, Apis, Niobe, and their descendants. Phoroneus ruled the land later called the Peloponnese and fathered Apis and Niobe, while Apis was killed after ruling as a stern tyrant and was regarded as the god Sarapis. Niobe had Argos by Zeus, and Argos later ruled the kingdom, naming the Peloponnese after himself and fathering several children. The lineage also includes Argus the All-seeing, who possessed eyes throughout his body, performed heroic deeds, and avenged the killing of Apis.

l: Inachus, The Library, BOOK ITI
s: Inachus was the son of Ocean and Tethys. A river in Argos was called Inachus after him, and he and Melia, daughter of Ocean, had Phoroneus and Aegialeus.

l: Phoroneus, The Library, BOOK ITI
s: Phoroneus was a son of Inachus and Melia. He ruled over the whole land later called the Peloponnese and fathered Apis and Niobe by the nymph Teledice.

l: Peloponnese, The Library, BOOK ITI
s: The land later called the Peloponnese was ruled by Phoroneus. Apis named it Apia after himself, and Argos later named it Argos after himself.

l: Apis, The Library, BOOK ITI
s: Apis was the son of Phoroneus and Teledice's fellow child with Niobe. He converted his power into a tyranny, named the Peloponnese Apia, and was killed in a conspiracy by Thelxion and Telchis; because he was regarded as a god, he was called Sarapis.

l: Niobe, The Library, BOOK ITI
s: Niobe was the daughter of Phoroneus and the nymph Teledice. She had Argos by Zeus and, according to Acusilaus, also had Pelasgus by him.

l: Zeus, The Library, BOOK ITI
s: Zeus had a son, Argos, by Niobe, who was the first mortal woman with whom Zeus cohabited according to the text. The text also attributes Pelasgus to Zeus and Niobe according to Acusilaus.

l: Argus, The Library, BOOK ITI
s: Argus was the son of Niobe and Zeus. After receiving the kingdom, he named the Peloponnese Argos after himself, married Evadne, and fathered Ecbasus, Peirantes, Epidaurus, and Criassus.

l: Argos, The Library, BOOK ITI
s: Argos was the name Argus gave to the Peloponnese after taking the kingdom. The name also designates the place associated with Inachus, after whom its river was called Inachus.

l: Argus the All-seeing, The Library, BOOK ITI
s: Argus the All-seeing was descended from Ecbasus through Agenor. He had eyes throughout his body and killed a bull ravaging Arcadia, a satyr harming the Arcadians, and Tartarus and Echidna while Echidna was asleep; he also avenged the killing of Apis by killing those responsible.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: This unit concerns Io’s transformation into a cow, her wanderings under Hera’s persecution, and her return to human form in Egypt, where she gives birth to Epaphus. It traces the descendants of Epaphus through Libya, Agenor, and Belus to Egyptus and Danaus, whose descendants become involved in a forced marriage alliance. Danaus’s daughters kill the sons of Egyptus on their wedding night, except for Hypermnestra, who spares Lynceus. The account also describes Amymone’s encounter with Poseidon and the origins of the springs at Lerna.

l: Argus the All-seeing, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Hera appointed Argus the All-seeing to guard Io after Zeus transformed her into a white cow. Argus tethered Io to an olive tree in the grove of the Mycenaeans, but Hermes killed him with a stone after Hierax revealed Hermes’s attempt to steal the cow; this is why Hermes was called Argiphontes.

l: Io, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Io was variously said to be the daughter of Iasus, Inachus, or Piren, and she held the priesthood of Hera when Zeus seduced her. Zeus changed her into a white cow, Hera had Argus guard her, and Hera later sent a gadfly to torment her. Io wandered through Europe and Asia before reaching Egypt, where she recovered her human form, gave birth to Epaphus, married Telegonus, and was identified with Isis.

l: Hera, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Hera detected Zeus’s seduction of Io and obtained Io from him in the form of a white cow. She appointed Argus the All-seeing to guard Io, sent a gadfly to torment her, and later asked the Curetes to make away with Epaphus.

l: Zeus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Zeus seduced Io and transformed her into a white cow when Hera discovered them. He ordered Hermes to steal Io, killed the Curetes after they made away with Epaphus, and later commanded Athena and Hermes to purify the daughters of Danaus.

l: Hermes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Zeus ordered Hermes to steal Io from Argus, but Hierax had revealed the attempt, so Hermes killed Argus with a stone. At Zeus’s command, Hermes also purified the daughters of Danaus together with Athena.

l: Egypt, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Egypt was the name given to the country after Egyptus, who subjugated the country of the Melampods and named it after himself.

l: Epaphus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Epaphus was born to Io beside the river Nile after Io recovered her original form in Egypt. Hera asked the Curetes to make him disappear, but Zeus killed the Curetes after learning what they had done. Epaphus was later found by Io, reigned over the Egyptians, married Memphis, founded Memphis after her, and fathered Libya.

l: Poseidon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Poseidon dried up the springs because he was angry with Inachus for testifying that the country belonged to Hera. He appeared when a satyr threatened Amymone, slept with her, and revealed to her the springs at Lerna.

l: Belus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Belus was the son of Libya and Poseidon and the twin brother of Agenor. He remained in Egypt, reigned over the country, married Anchinoe, daughter of Nile, and fathered the twins Egyptus and Danaus.

l: Egyptus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Egyptus was the son of Belus and Anchinoe and the twin brother of Danaus. He was settled in Arabia, conquered the country of the Melampods, and had fifty sons by several women. His sons later came to Argos and sought to marry the daughters of Danaus.

l: Danaus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Danaus was the son of Belus and Anchinoe and the twin brother of Egyptus. Fearing Egyptus’s sons after a quarrel over the kingdom, he built a ship on Athena’s advice, fled with his fifty daughters, and eventually reached Argos, where he became king and named the inhabitants Danai. He agreed to marry his daughters to the sons of Egyptus but gave the daughters daggers and later arranged athletic contests for their remarriage.

l: sons of Egyptus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: The fifty sons of Egyptus came to Argos, asked Danaus to end the hostility, and sought to marry his daughters. Danaus allotted the marriages among them, but the sons were killed by their brides while they slept, except for Lynceus.

l: daughters of Danaus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: The fifty daughters of Danaus fled with him to Argos and were allotted as brides to the sons of Egyptus. All but Hypermnestra killed their bridegrooms while they slept; they later buried the heads at Lerna and honored the bodies before the city, and Athena and Hermes purified them at Zeus’s command.

l: Amymone, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Amymone, one of Danaus’s daughters, searched for water in the drought-stricken country and accidentally struck a sleeping satyr with a dart aimed at a deer. Poseidon intervened when the satyr attacked her, slept with her, and showed her the springs at Lerna. Amymone later bore Nauplius to Poseidon.

l: Lynceus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Lynceus was one of the sons of Egyptus and was allotted Hypermnestra as his bride. Hypermnestra spared him because he had respected her virginity, and Danaus later united them in marriage.

l: Hypermnestra, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: Hypermnestra was the eldest daughter of Danaus and was allotted to Lynceus. She spared Lynceus when the other daughters killed their bridegrooms because he had respected her virginity; Danaus imprisoned her but later united her with Lynceus.

l: mass killing of the bridegrooms, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. 1. 1-3
s: After Danaus agreed to the marriages, he gave his daughters daggers, and they killed the sons of Egyptus while the bridegrooms slept. Hypermnestra alone did not participate, because she spared Lynceus; the other daughters buried the bridegrooms’ heads at Lerna and honored their bodies before the city.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Proetus occupied Tiryns after his father-in-law restored him, while he and Acrisius divided the Argive territory, with Acrisius ruling Argos and Proetus ruling Tiryns. Proetus's daughters and the other Argive women were seized by madness, and Melampus cured the surviving daughters after Proetus agreed to his demands for land. Bellerophon came to Proetus for purification after accidentally killing a relative, but Stheneboea falsely accused him of making improper advances. Proetus sent Bellerophon to Iobates with a letter ordering his death, but Iobates instead assigned him dangerous campaigns, which Bellerophon completed with the aid of Pegasus and ultimately won Iobates's admiration and kingdom.

l: Acrisius, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Acrisius divided the Argive territory with Proetus and reigned over Argos. He had a daughter, Danae, by Eurydice, daughter of Lacedaemon.

l: Proetus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Proetus was restored to his land by his father-in-law and occupied Tiryns, which the Cyclopes had fortified. He had three daughters by Stheneboea, agreed to Melampus's terms for curing the women, and later sent Bellerophon to Iobates with a letter ordering Bellerophon's death.

l: Argos, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Argos was part of the Argive territory divided between Acrisius and Proetus, and Acrisius reigned over it.

l: Iobates, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Iobates received Bellerophon and the letter from Proetus ordering Bellerophon's death. Instead of killing him directly, he assigned Bellerophon the tasks of killing the Chimera, fighting the Solymi and the Amazons, and ambushing the bravest Lycians; after Bellerophon succeeded, Iobates showed him the letter, asked him to remain, gave him his daughter Philonoe, and left him the kingdom when he died.

l: Stheneboea, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Stheneboea fell in love with Bellerophon and sent him proposals for a meeting. When he rejected them, she falsely told Proetus that Bellerophon had made improper advances to her.

l: Tiryns, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Tiryns was occupied by Proetus after his father-in-law restored him, and the Cyclopes had fortified it for him. Proetus reigned over Tiryns after the division of the Argive territory.

l: Melampus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Melampus, son of Amythaon and Idmene, was a seer who was the first to devise a cure by drugs and purifications. He agreed to cure Proetus's daughters in exchange for a third of the sovereignty and later pursued the women to Sicyon, where the surviving daughters were purified and recovered their wits.

l: Bellerophon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Bellerophon came to Proetus for purification after accidentally killing a relative. He rejected Stheneboea, survived the tasks assigned by Iobates, killed the Chimera and the Lycians sent against him, and received Philonoe and the kingdom from Iobates.

l: Chimera, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: The Chimera had the forepart of a lion, the tail of a dragon, and a goat's middle head, which belched fire. It devastated the country and harried the cattle until Bellerophon shot it down from the height while riding Pegasus.

l: Pegasus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Pegasus was a winged horse born from Medusa and Poseidon. Bellerophon rode Pegasus into the air and used the height to shoot down the Chimera.

l: madness of the Argive women, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Proetus's daughters went mad because, according to Hesiod, they refused the rites of Dionysus, or, according to Acusilaus, because they disparaged the wooden image of Hera. Their madness spread to the other women, who abandoned their homes, destroyed their children, and went into the desert.

l: purification and cure, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Melampus promised to cure the maddened women through drugs and purifications in return for a share of the sovereignty. During the pursuit to Sicyon, Iphinoe died, while the other daughters were purified and recovered their wits.

l: letter to Iobates, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Proetus gave Bellerophon a letter to carry to Iobates, and the letter ordered Iobates to kill Bellerophon. Iobates showed the letter to Bellerophon only after Bellerophon had completed the assigned campaigns.

l: Bellerophon's campaigns, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 11. 1. 5—u. 1
s: Iobates ordered Bellerophon to kill the Chimera, fight the Solymi, fight the Amazons, and ambush the reputedly bravest Lycians. Bellerophon completed every task and killed the enemies sent against him.

l: The Library, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Acrisius learned from an oracle that Danae would bear a son who would kill him, so he confined Danae, but she gave birth to Perseus. Acrisius cast Danae and Perseus into the sea in a chest, and Dictys rescued and raised Perseus on Seriphus, where Polydectes later sent Perseus to obtain the Gorgon’s head. Guided by Hermes and Athena, Perseus obtained magical equipment from the nymphs, decapitated Medusa, and traveled to Ethiopia, where he found Andromeda exposed to a sea monster.

l: Acrisius, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Acrisius learned from an oracle that Danae would bear a son who would kill him. He confined Danae, then cast her and Perseus into the sea in a chest.

l: Danae, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Danae was confined by Acrisius in a brazen chamber. She was seduced by Proetus according to one account, or had intercourse with Zeus in the form of gold according to another, and gave birth to Perseus.

l: Zeus, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Zeus had intercourse with Danae, according to one account, after transforming himself into gold that poured through the roof into her lap.

l: Perseus, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Perseus was cast into the sea with Danae, rescued and raised by Dictys, and later ordered by Polydectes to bring the Gorgon’s head. With guidance from Hermes and Athena, he obtained magical equipment, decapitated Medusa, and traveled to Ethiopia.

l: Dictys, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Dictys took up the chest when it reached Seriphus and raised Perseus.

l: Polydectes, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Polydectes, king of Seriphus and Dictys’s brother, fell in love with Danae. He contrived to send Perseus after the Gorgon’s head.

l: Seriphus, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Seriphus was the place where the chest came ashore. Polydectes ruled there, and Dictys raised Perseus there.

l: Hermes, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Hermes guided Perseus toward the Phorcides and gave him an adamantine sickle.

l: Athena, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Athena guided Perseus toward the Phorcides and directed his hand while he decapitated Medusa, allowing him to use a bronze shield to see her reflection.

l: the Phorcides, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: The Phorcides were Enyo, Pephredo, and Dino, daughters of Phorcus and Ceto and sisters of the Gorgons. They shared one eye and one tooth, and showed Perseus the way to the nymphs after he took possession of them.

l: the nymphs, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: The nymphs possessed winged sandals, the wallet, and the cap of Hades. They gave Perseus the equipment he sought after the Phorcides directed him to them.

l: Medusa, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Medusa was the only mortal among the Gorgons. Perseus found her asleep and decapitated her; Pegasus and Chrysaor sprang from her after her head was cut off.

l: the Gorgons, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: The Gorgons were Stheno, Euryale, and Medusa. Their heads were covered with dragon scales, and they had tusks like swine, brazen hands, and golden wings; they turned those who saw them to stone.

l: Ethiopia, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Ethiopia was ruled by Cepheus. Perseus arrived there and found Andromeda exposed as food for a sea monster.

l: Cepheus, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Cepheus ruled Ethiopia and was the father of Andromeda and the husband of Cassiopeia. He was forced by the Ethiopians to expose Andromeda to the sea monster.

l: Andromeda, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Andromeda, daughter of Cepheus and Cassiopeia, was exposed as food for a sea monster and fastened to a rock. Perseus saw her and fell in love with her.

l: Cassiopeia, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Cassiopeia, wife of Cepheus and mother of Andromeda, claimed to be more beautiful than the Nereids. The Nereids became angry because of this claim.

l: the Nereids, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: The Nereids became angry with Cassiopeia after she claimed superiority in beauty. Poseidon shared their anger and sent a flood and a sea monster against the land.

l: Poseidon, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Poseidon shared the Nereids’ anger at Cassiopeia and sent a flood and a sea monster against the land.

l: the sea monster, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: The sea monster was sent against the land by Poseidon. It was to receive Andromeda as food after the oracle of Ammon declared that this would end the disaster.

l: the chest, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Acrisius put Danae and Perseus into a chest and cast it into the sea. The chest was washed ashore on Seriphus, where Dictys took it up.

l: the winged sandals, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: The winged sandals belonged to the nymphs. Perseus received them from the nymphs and fitted them to his ankles.

l: wallet (kibisis), The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: The wallet, called the kibisis, belonged to the nymphs and was used for carrying the Gorgon’s head. Perseus received it and slung it around himself.

l: the cap of Hades, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: The cap of Hades belonged to the nymphs. When Perseus wore it, he could see whom he wished while remaining unseen by others.

l: Gorgon’s head, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Polydectes ordered Perseus to bring the Gorgon’s head. Perseus placed Medusa’s head in the wallet after decapitating her.

l: the prophecy about Acrisius, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: The oracle told Acrisius that Danae would give birth to a son who would kill him. Acrisius feared this prophecy and confined Danae.

l: Danae’s seduction by Zeus, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: According to one account, Zeus seduced Danae by transforming into gold that poured through the roof into her lap. This union produced Perseus.

l: the casting of Danae and Perseus into the sea, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Acrisius put Danae and Perseus into a chest and cast them into the sea because he had learned that Danae had borne Perseus.

l: Perseus’s quest for the Gorgon’s head, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Polydectes sent Perseus to obtain the Gorgon’s head after Perseus declared that he would not refuse even that task. Hermes and Athena guided him, and the nymphs supplied the equipment he needed.

l: the decapitation of Medusa, The Library, IV. When Acrisius inquired of the oracle how he .. Παραγενόμενος δὲ εἰς Αἰθιοπίαν, ἧς ἐβασίλευε
s: Perseus decapitated the sleeping Medusa while looking at her image in a bronze shield and following Athena’s direction. Pegasus and Chrysaor sprang from Medusa after her head was cut off.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Perseus beheaded Medusa with Athena’s guidance, rescued Andromeda from a sea monster, and turned Phineus and his fellow conspirators to stone with the Gorgon’s head. He returned to Seriphus, turned Polydectes and his gathered friends to stone, made Dictys king, and gave the Gorgon’s head to Athena. Perseus later caused the death of Acrisius by accidentally striking him with a quoit, exchanged Argos with Megapenthes, and ruled Tiryns while fortifying Midea and Mycenae. The unit also recounts the lineage of Perseus, including Electryon, Amphitryon, Alcmena, and the events leading to Electryon’s accidental death.

l: Perseus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Perseus beheaded Medusa with Athena’s guidance, rescued Andromeda by killing the sea monster, and turned Phineus and his fellow conspirators to stone with the Gorgon’s head. He returned to Seriphus, turned Polydectes and his friends to stone, made Dictys king, and gave the Gorgon’s head to Athena. After accidentally killing Acrisius with a quoit, he exchanged Argos with Megapenthes and ruled Tiryns, fortifying Midea and Mycenae.

l: Athena, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Athena guided Perseus’s hand as he looked at Medusa’s image in a brazen shield. Perseus later gave her the Gorgon’s head, which she placed in the middle of her shield.

l: Medusa, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Medusa was beheaded by Perseus while Athena guided him and he viewed her image in a brazen shield. From her body sprang Pegasus and Chrysaor, whom she had by Poseidon.

l: Andromeda, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Andromeda was exposed as prey for a sea monster and bound to a rock because of the calamity sent against the land. Perseus rescued her by killing the monster, married her, and had children with her.

l: Gorgon’s head, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Perseus used the Gorgon’s head to turn Phineus and his fellow conspirators, Polydectes, and Polydectes’s friends to stone. He gave it to Athena, who placed it in the middle of her shield.

l: Acrisius, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Acrisius fled Argos because he feared the oracle concerning Danae’s son. Perseus accidentally killed him by striking his foot with a quoit during a pentathlon, and buried him outside the city.

l: Electryon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Electryon ruled Mycenae and committed the kingdom and Alcmena to Amphitryon while planning war against the Teleboans. Amphitryon accidentally killed him when a club rebounded from a cow’s horns and struck his head.

l: Amphitryon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Amphitryon received the kingdom and Alcmena from Electryon, with an oath to keep her a virgin until Electryon returned. While recovering the cattle, he threw a club at a charging cow, and its rebound killed Electryon; Sthenelus then banished him.

l: Alcmena, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Alcmena was given to Amphitryon along with the kingdom by Electryon, who required Amphitryon to keep her a virgin until his return. She later declared that she would marry Amphitryon only after he avenged the death of her brothers.

l: Argos, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Perseus went toward Argos to see Acrisius, but after Acrisius fled, Perseus later exchanged Argos with Megapenthes. Megapenthes then ruled over the Argives.

l: Mycenae, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Eurystheus reigned over Mycenae, and Perseus later ruled there after fortifying it. Electryon also ruled Mycenae until his death.

l: Medusa’s beheading, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Medusa’s beheading was carried out by Perseus with Athena guiding his hand while he looked at her image in a brazen shield. Some accounts in the text say that Medusa was beheaded for Athena’s sake because the Gorgon had wished to compete with Athena in beauty.

l: Andromeda’s rescue, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: Andromeda’s rescue occurred when Perseus promised Cepheus to kill the sea monster in exchange for marrying her. Perseus killed the monster and released Andromeda, but then faced the plot of Phineus, her former betrothed.

l: death of Acrisius, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: The death of Acrisius occurred during athletic games held by Teutamides of Larissa. Perseus, competing in the pentathlon, accidentally struck Acrisius’s foot with a quoit and killed him, fulfilling the oracle.

l: Electryon's death, The Library, THE LIBRARY, 1]. 1v. 2-3
s: The death of Electryon occurred when Amphitryon threw a club at a cow that had charged while the cattle were being recovered. The club rebounded from the cow’s horns and struck Electryon’s head, killing him.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Amphitryon went to Thebes with Alcmena and Licymnius, was purified by Creon, and undertook to avenge Alcmena’s brothers so that he could marry her. Creon agreed to assist Amphitryon against the Teleboans if Amphitryon first rid the Cadmea of the Teumessian vixen, but the vixen was fated never to be caught. Amphitryon brought Cephalus and the dog Laelaps to hunt the vixen, and Zeus turned both animals into stones. Amphitryon then conquered the Tafian islands after Comaetho removed the golden lock from Pterelaus’s head, causing Pterelaus to die.

l: Amphitryon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Amphitryon went with Alcmena and Licymnius to Thebes and was purified by Creon. He undertook to avenge Alcmena’s brothers, tried to rid the Cadmea of the vixen, and then led an expedition against the Teleboans. He later conquered the Tafian islands and killed Comaetho.

l: Alcmena, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Alcmena said that she would marry Amphitryon after he had avenged the deaths of her brothers.

l: Creon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Creon purified Amphitryon at Thebes and agreed to assist his expedition against the Teleboans if Amphitryon first rid the Cadmea of the vixen. He joined Amphitryon in the attack on the Tafian islands.

l: Thebes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Thebes was where Amphitryon, Alcmena, and Licymnius went, and where Amphitryon was purified. The Thebans suffered from the vixen and exposed one citizen’s son each month to prevent it from carrying off many people.

l: the Teleboans, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: The Teleboans were the target of Amphitryon’s expedition, which he undertook after agreeing to avenge Alcmena’s brothers.

l: expedition against the Teleboans, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Amphitryon undertook the expedition against the Teleboans and invited Creon to assist him. He also promised a share of the spoils to those who joined him.

l: Cadmeia, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: The Cadmea was ravaged by the Teumessian vixen. Creon required Amphitryon to rid it of the animal before he would assist in the expedition against the Teleboans.

l: Teumessian vixen, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: The vixen ravaged the Cadmea, and it was fated that nobody could catch it. It was pursued by Laelaps until Zeus turned both animals into stones.

l: Cephalus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Cephalus joined Amphitryon from Athens and brought the dog Laelaps, which Procris had obtained from Minos. He received a share of the spoils from the Tafian islands and settled in a city founded under his name.

l: Laelaps, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Laelaps was the dog brought by Cephalus from Crete. It was fated to catch everything it pursued, and it chased the vixen until Zeus turned both animals into stones.

l: hunt for the vixen, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Amphitryon went to Athens and persuaded Cephalus to join the hunt with the dog Laelaps. The hunt ended when Zeus turned the pursuing dog and the vixen into stones.

l: Zeus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Zeus came to Thebes before Amphitryon returned, assuming Amphitryon’s likeness and greatly lengthening the night. He turned the vixen and Laelaps into stones when the dog pursued the vixen.

l: petrification of the vixen and dog, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: When Laelaps pursued the vixen, Zeus turned both the vixen and the dog into stones.

l: Tafian islands, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: The Tafian islands were attacked by Amphitryon with allies from Athens, Phocis, Argos, and Thebes. After Pterelaus died, Amphitryon conquered all the islands and distributed them among his companions.

l: Pterelaus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: The Tafian islands could not be conquered while Pterelaus was alive. After Comaetho removed the golden lock from his head, Pterelaus died and Amphitryon conquered the islands.

l: Comaetho, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Comaetho, the daughter of Pterelaus, fell in love with Amphitryon and removed the golden lock from her father’s head. After Pterelaus died, Amphitryon killed Comaetho.

l: golden lock of Pterelaus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: The golden lock was taken from Pterelaus’s head by his daughter Comaetho. Its removal caused Pterelaus to die.

l: conquest of the Tafian islands, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: Amphitryon’s conquest of the Tafian islands became possible after Comaetho removed the golden lock from Pterelaus’s head and Pterelaus died. Amphitryon then gave the islands as spoils to Cephalus and his other allies.

l: killing of Comaetho, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 6-7
s: After Comaetho caused Pterelaus’s death by removing the golden lock, Amphitryon killed her.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: Amphitryon’s campaigns and death are followed by Hercules’ marriage to Megara and his violent madness, during which he kills his children and two children of Iphicles. Hercules is purified and goes to Delphi, where the Delphic oracle gives him the name Hercules and orders him to serve Eurystheus at Tiryns for twelve years and perform ten labours. The first labour requires Hercules to bring back the hide of the invulnerable Nemean lion, which he goes to hunt.

l: Zeus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: Zeus is identified as the father of Hercules, who receives divine gifts including a sword from Hermes, a bow and arrows from Apollo, a golden breastplate from Hephaestus, and a robe from Athena.

l: Amphitryon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: Amphitryon dies fighting bravely in the battle against the Minyans. Hercules later receives Megara from Creon after this conflict.

l: Thebes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: Thebes had been required to send Erginus a yearly tribute of one hundred cattle for twenty years. After Hercules kills Erginus and defeats the Minyans, he compels the Minyans to pay double the tribute to Thebes.

l: Alcmena, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: Alcmena is later married by Rhadamanthys, son of Zeus, after the death of Amphitryon.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: Hercules receives weapons and equipment from several gods and uses a club that he cut himself at Nemea. After killing his children in a fit of madness, he is purified by Thespius, goes to Delphi, and is directed to serve Eurystheus at Tiryns for twelve years while performing ten labours.

l: Hera, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: Hera’s jealousy causes Hercules to become mad after the battle with the Minyans.

l: Erginus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: Erginus marches against Thebes after Hercules mutilates his heralds. Hercules kills Erginus, defeats the Minyans, and reverses the tribute imposed on Thebes.

l: the madness of Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: The madness of Hercules is attributed to Hera’s jealousy and occurs after the battle with the Minyans. During it, Hercules throws his own children by Megara and two children of Iphicles into a fire.

l: the killing of Hercules' children, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: The killing of Hercules' children occurs during his madness after the battle with the Minyans. Hercules also kills two children of Iphicles and thereafter condemns himself to exile.

l: Delphi, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: Hercules goes to Delphi after being purified by Thespius and asks where he should dwell.

l: oracle of Apollo, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: The Delphic oracle first calls Alcides by the name Hercules. It directs him to live at Tiryns, serve Eurystheus for twelve years, and complete ten labours in order to become immortal.

l: Tiryns, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: Tiryns is designated as the place where Hercules must live while serving Eurystheus for twelve years.

l: Eurystheus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: Eurystheus commands Hercules to perform the labours. His first command is that Hercules bring back the hide of the Nemean lion.

l: the labours of Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: The labours of Hercules are ten tasks imposed by Eurystheus, to be performed during twelve years at Tiryns. The completion of the labours is said to lead to Hercules becoming immortal.

l: the Nemean lion, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: The Nemean lion is an invulnerable animal born from Typhon. Hercules travels to hunt it after Eurystheus commands him to bring back its hide.

l: the Nemean lion labour, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. tv. 7-8
s: The Nemean lion labour is the first task assigned to Hercules by Eurystheus. Hercules must bring back the lion’s hide and goes to Cleonae, where he stays with Molorchus before hunting it.

l: The Library, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: Hercules carries out the first five labours ordered by Eurystheus, including killing the Nemean lion and the Lernaean hydra, capturing the Cerynitian hind and the Erymanthian boar, and undertaking the cleaning of the Augean cattle’s stalls. Eurystheus forbids Hercules from entering Mycenae and orders him to display his labours before the gates. Iolaus assists Hercules against the hydra, so Eurystheus refuses to count that labour among the ten. The unit also recounts Hercules’ encounters with Artemis, the centaurs, and Augeias.

l: Hercules, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: Hercules obeys Eurystheus and performs the labours assigned to him. He kills the Nemean lion, defeats the Lernaean hydra with Iolaus’s help, captures the Cerynitian hind alive, captures the Erymanthian boar alive, and is ordered to remove the dung of the Augean cattle in one day.

l: Eurystheus, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: Eurystheus orders Hercules to perform the labours. After seeing the Nemean lion, he is so afraid of Hercules’ strength that he forbids him to enter the city and orders him to display the labours before the gates; he also refuses to count the hydra among the ten because Iolaus helped.

l: the labours of Hercules, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: The unit describes the first five labours: the Nemean lion, the Lernaean hydra, the Cerynitian hind, the Erymanthian boar, and the Augean cattle. Eurystheus assigns these tasks to Hercules, though he excludes the hydra from the ten because Hercules received help from Iolaus.

l: the Nemean lion, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: The Nemean lion is an invulnerable beast begotten by Typhon. Hercules drives it into a two-mouthed cave, blocks one entrance, chokes it through the other, and carries its body to Mycenae.

l: Mycenae, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: Mycenae is where Hercules brings the Nemean lion and the living Cerynitian hind. Eurystheus resides there and orders Hercules to display his labours before the city gates rather than enter the city.

l: the Lernaean hydra, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: The Lernaean hydra lives in the swamp of Lerna and ravages the cattle and countryside. It has nine heads, eight mortal and one immortal; Hercules and Iolaus defeat it, bury the immortal head beneath a rock, and Hercules dips his arrows in its gall.

l: Iolaus, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: Iolaus drives the chariot that carries Hercules to Lerna and helps him defeat the hydra. He burns the roots of the severed heads so that they cannot grow back, leading Eurystheus to reject the labour as one completed by Hercules alone.

l: the Cerynitian hind, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: The Cerynitian hind has golden horns and is sacred to Artemis. Hercules pursues it for a year, captures it alive near the river Ladon, appeases Artemis by blaming Eurystheus, and carries it to Mycenae.

l: the Erymanthian boar, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: The Erymanthian boar ravages Psophis from Mount Erymanthus. Hercules pursues it through deep snow, captures it with a noose, and carries it alive to Mycenae.

l: the Augean cattle, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: The Augean cattle belong to Augeias, who has many herds. Eurystheus orders Hercules to remove their dung in a single day.

l: Augeas, The Library, V. When Hercules heard that, he went to Tiryns
s: Augeias is king of Elis and possesses many herds of cattle. Hercules approaches him and says he can remove the dung in one day if Augeias gives him a tenth of the cattle; Augeias agrees because he does not believe Hercules can accomplish it.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: Hercules completes the fifth through eighth labours by cleansing Augeas's cattle-yard, driving away the Stymphalian birds, bringing the Cretan Bull to Eurystheus, and capturing Diomedes's man-eating mares. Eurystheus rejects the fifth labour because Hercules performed it for a promised reward, and he also rejects an additional deed involving Eurytion for the same reason. Hercules then undertakes the ninth labour, traveling to the Amazons to obtain Hippolyte's belt of Ares. At Troy, Hercules encounters a city suffering under the wrath of Apollo and Poseidon.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: Hercules diverts the Alpheus and Peneus into Augeas's cattle-yard and cleanses it in a single day. He drives away the Stymphalian birds, brings the Cretan Bull to Eurystheus, captures Diomedes's mares, and later sails to obtain Hippolyte's belt. At Themiscyra he kills Hippolyte after suspecting treachery, fights the Amazons, and then touches at Troy.

l: Eurystheus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: Eurystheus assigns the fifth through ninth labours to Hercules. He refuses to count the cleansing of Augeas's cattle-yard and Hercules's killing of Eurytion among the ten because they were performed for hire, but he receives the Cretan Bull and the man-eating mares.

l: fifth labour, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: The fifth labour requires Hercules to carry out the dung from Augeas's cattle-yard in a single day. Hercules completes it by diverting the Alpheus and Peneus through the yard, but Eurystheus does not accept it because Hercules had undertaken it for a promised reward.

l: Augeas, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: Augeas is king of Elis and possesses many herds of cattle. He promises Hercules a tenth of the cattle for cleansing the yard, then denies the promise after learning that the task was commanded by Eurystheus and expels Hercules and Phyleus.

l: Poseidon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: Poseidon is named as one possible father of Augeas. In another account, he sends the Cretan Bull from the sea, and he later joins Apollo in bringing distress upon Troy because Laomedon failed to pay them.

l: sixth labour, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: The sixth labour requires Hercules to chase away the Stymphalian birds. Athena gives him brazen castanets, which he uses to frighten the birds into flight so that he can shoot them.

l: Stymphalian birds, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: The Stymphalian birds gather in the wooded lake at Stymphalus, fearing attack by wolves. The sound of Athena's brazen castanets drives them into the air, where Hercules shoots them.

l: seventh labour, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: The seventh labour requires Hercules to bring the Cretan Bull. He captures it after Minos tells him to fight for it himself, brings it to Eurystheus, and then releases it.

l: Cretan Bull, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: The Cretan Bull is variously identified as the bull that carried Europa to Zeus or the bull that Poseidon sent from the sea. After Hercules releases it, it wanders through Sparta and Arcadia, crosses the Isthmus, and reaches Marathon, where it harms the inhabitants.

l: eighth labour, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: The eighth labour requires Hercules to bring the mares of Diomedes to Mycenae. He captures them, but they kill Abderus while he is guarding them; Hercules then kills Diomedes, subdues the Bistones, and delivers the mares to Eurystheus.

l: Diomedes, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: Diomedes is a Thracian king, son of Ares and Cyrene, and ruler of the Bistones. He owns man-eating mares, and Hercules kills him during the fighting that follows the mares' capture.

l: man-eating mares, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: The man-eating mares belong to Diomedes and are kept at their mangers. They kill Abderus by dragging him after them, are brought by Hercules to Eurystheus, and are later released and destroyed by wild beasts on Mount Olympus.

l: ninth labour, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: The ninth labour requires Hercules to bring Hippolyte's belt. He sails with volunteer comrades to the Amazons, reaches Themiscyra, and takes the belt after killing Hippolyte and fighting the Amazons.

l: Hippolyte, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: Hippolyte is queen of the Amazons and possesses the belt of Ares as a symbol of her supremacy. She meets Hercules at Themiscyra, promises to give him the belt, but is killed by him when Hera incites the Amazons and Hercules suspects treachery.

l: Amazons, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: The Amazons dwell around the Thermodon and are described as a large, warlike people. After Hera claims that the visiting strangers will abduct their queen, the Amazons ride armed toward Hercules's ship, fight him, and are defeated.

l: belt of Hippolyta, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: The belt of Ares belongs to Hippolyte and signifies her superiority over all the Amazons. Hercules obtains it after killing Hippolyte during the conflict at Themiscyra.

l: Troy, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: Hercules touches at Troy after fighting the Amazons. At that time the city is suffering because of the anger of Apollo and Poseidon.

l: Apollo, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: Apollo and Poseidon once agree to build the walls of Troy for Laomedon in return for payment. When Laomedon fails to pay them, Apollo sends a plague against the city.

l: Laomedon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 4-5
s: Laomedon is the ruler of Troy. He fails to pay Apollo and Poseidon after they build the city's walls, and the resulting divine anger brings a plague and a sea monster against Troy.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Apollo and Poseidon assumed human form and fortified Pergamum for Laomedon in return for wages, but Laomedon refused to pay them. Apollo sent a pestilence and Poseidon sent a sea monster that carried away people from the plain, and Laomedon exposed his daughter Hesione to it after oracles promised deliverance. Hercules offered to rescue Hesione in exchange for the horses Zeus had given to Tros, killed the sea monster, and saved her. When Laomedon again refused payment, Hercules threatened to wage war on Troy.

l: Laomedon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Laomedon hired Apollo and Poseidon to fortify Pergamum but refused to pay their wages. He exposed his daughter Hesione to the sea monster after oracles foretold that this would deliver the people from the pestilence and the monster, and he later refused to pay Hercules as well.

l: Apollo, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Apollo assumed the likeness of a man with Poseidon and fortified Pergamum for Laomedon in return for wages. After Laomedon refused to pay, Apollo sent a pestilence.

l: Poseidon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Poseidon assumed the likeness of a man with Apollo and fortified Pergamum for Laomedon in return for wages. After Laomedon refused to pay, Poseidon sent a sea monster.

l: wages, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Laomedon promised wages to Apollo and Poseidon for fortifying Pergamum but refused to pay them. Hercules also expected payment after rescuing Hesione, but Laomedon refused to give it.

l: sea monster (Hesione's captor), The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Poseidon sent the sea monster after Laomedon refused to pay. Carried inland by a flood, it snatched away the people of the plain, and Hesione was exposed to it until Hercules killed it.

l: Hesione, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Hesione was Laomedon's daughter. Laomedon fastened her to rocks near the sea to be devoured by the sea monster, but Hercules rescued her.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Hercules promised to rescue Hesione if he received the horses that Zeus had given to Tros. He killed the sea monster and saved Hesione, then threatened to wage war on Troy when Laomedon refused to pay him.

l: horses of Tros, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: The horses of Tros were promised to Hercules as payment for rescuing Hesione. The text states that Zeus had given them as a penalty for the abduction of Ganymede.

l: Zeus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Zeus gave the horses of Tros as a penalty for the abduction of Ganymede.

l: Troy, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Hercules threatened to wage war on Troy after Laomedon refused to give him the promised payment.

l: rescue of Hesione, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Hercules's rescue of Hesione was secured by his killing the sea monster. He undertook the rescue in exchange for the horses of Tros.

l: The Library, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Hercules undertakes his tenth labour by fetching the red kine of Geryon from Erythia. He crosses the ocean in a golden goblet given to him by the Sun, kills Geryon, Eurytion, and Orthus, and drives the kine through Europe and Italy. After recovering an escaped bull from Eryx and overcoming Hera's dispersal of the herd, Hercules brings the kine to Eurystheus. Eurystheus sacrifices the kine to Hera.

l: Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Hercules is ordered to fetch the red kine of Geryon. He travels to Erythia, kills Orthus, Eurytion, and Geryon, crosses the ocean in a golden goblet, recovers an escaped bull from Eryx, and eventually brings the kine to Eurystheus.

l: Eurystheus, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Eurystheus receives the kine brought back by Hercules and sacrifices them to Hera.

l: Geryon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Geryon inhabits Erythia and owns the red kine. After learning that Hercules is taking them, he attacks Hercules beside the river Anthemus and is shot dead.

l: tenth labour of Hercules, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: The tenth labour of Hercules is to fetch the kine of Geryon from Erythia.

l: Erythia, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: Erythia is an island near the ocean, now called Gadira. It is inhabited by Geryon and is the place where Geryon's red kine are kept.

l: red kine of Geryon, The Library, THE LIBRARY, II. v. 9
s: The red kine belong to Geryon and are guarded by Eurytion and Orthus. Hercules takes them from Erythia, drives them across many lands, recovers some after they scatter, and delivers them to Eurystheus.
